Then we can re-scale {c Wj}j∈J0 using the estimated heteroskedasticity and recover the distribution of W1.18 This approach is asymptotically valid in settings with N0 →∞ and N1 fixed (even when N1 = 1) if we assume a scale-change model for the distribution of Wj = ξj × σ(Xj), where ξj is iid across treated and control units, but V(Wj) depends on a set of observed covariates, Xj. In particular, in the example in which Yj,t represents state × time aggregates, this approach corrects for the fact that the errors of the treated state should have a higher variance than the errors of the control states, if the treated state is relatively smaller. Inference methods based on sign-changes method have been considered in DiD settings with few treated and many control units when we have uniform treatment timing (Canay et al., 2017). Relatively to the methods from Section 4.1.1 and 4.1.2, this approach requires access to individual-level data, and it requires the use of a CLT within cluster (so it precludes, for example, cluster-level shocks, which are allowed by these other methods).29 In a comparison of means setting with one treated and one control cluster, Leung’s approach to inference relies on a standard two-sample t-test statistic, with the average in each cluster being computed by randomly resampling Rj units with replacement from each cluster j. results.content: 3.2 Equal Cluster Sizes Our most important, and most surprising, result is that the ordinary wild bootstrap can yield approximately valid inferences even when G1 is very small, provided all cluster sizes are the same, so that Ng = N/G. The results in Figure 5, together with additional ones for larger values of G1 and other values of ρ, suggest that, when cluster sizes are equal, it is better to use the ordinary wild bootstrap than to subcluster at any level.
